evidence: Traupman 51, 286: crux, the suit of clubs
terms.comment: Classically the gibbet; in Christian Latin the Cross, and so the shape. For a child drawing, two lines, one across the other, make a crux.

terms.gloss: an X, the crossing of two lines in the shape of the numeral ten
terms.comment: From the Roman numeral X, ten assēs: two lines crossing slantwise. Its verb is decussō, to cross in the form of an X (Col. 3.13), and the adverb decussātim, crosswise (Vitr. 1.6, Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: Dūc līneam ab summō ad īmum, deinde alteram trānsversam: ecce crux!
phrases.english: Draw a line from top to bottom, then another across it: there’s a cross!

phrases.latin: duās rēgulās ejus lātitūdinis, quā pastinātor sulcum factūrus est, in speciem Graecae litterae X decussāvimus
phrases.english: we crossed two rulers, as wide as the digger is going to make his trench, in the shape of the Greek letter X

sources: Lewis & Short: crux · Lewis & Short: decussis · Lewis & Short: decusso
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 51, 286.
